name: Things That Are Not in the Book
sub: the stranger creatures and entities of the Hide, by whoever met them and lived, or did not
epi: Each of these was met by someone who meant to write more.
preface:
Ten things that stand in no bestiary, by the ten who met them. I was present at none of the meetings. I say where I was.

The hospice book I had from the sister who took the broom after the matron; she gave me the leaves and kept the cloth.

The exorcist's ledger was in his coat when they found the coat, and the coat was on a peg a league from the rest of him, and the pedlar who sold me the ledger would not say which was found first.

The discrepancy was bound among the niche-tallies of the Fifth Ossuary, and a tallier copied it for me in return for a count I had and he wanted, and I gave him the number and kept the root.

The sacristan's inventory lay in the press of the monastery the pilgrims call Fallen, under ash that smelled of nothing, and I read it there and rang nothing.

The letter was folded in a bedroll made up beside a dead fire on the Barrow road. There was no one in the bedroll. I sat the night by it, and nobody came for it, three paces off or nearer.

The claim is a fair copy from the reeve's roll at Four Wents; the reeve lent it to me for the price of counting his carters, and I gave him the number he wanted.

The survey came to the Warden-Crone at Maren's camp with the cord wound round it. The cord is short by three knots. I have measured it.

The warden's report lay on his table at the Grieving Stone under a stone, with the rest of the leaf clean. His successor gave it to me rather than read it.

The shore-log I took from the hut at the Drowned Village myself, with a lantern on the step outside that was dark and was not mine.

The visitation went down the old water-cut with the Peak's youngest, with the abbot's letter, and the lowland priest who kept them both gave me this one and kept the other.

I have changed none of them. Where a hand changes, I have let it change. Where a page ends before its writer meant it to, so does mine.

pages.title: Intakes at the Hospice Below Sighing Ridge
pages.by: These are the last filled leaves of the intake book of the hospice below Sighing Ridge, in the matron's hand and then in another. The book was shut on a strip of grey cloth laid in it at this page for a marker. The sister who gave me the leaves kept the strip, and I did not argue, because it was warm.
pages.epi: Wrapped to the chin, well or ill, pilgrim or sister.
pages.bb:
[b]Intake eleven hundred and six.[/b] A woman of this house. Brought: on her own feet, at the lamp-hour. By: nobody. Complaint: cold. She says she is cold to the bone and that the bone is cold as well. Bed: she will take none. She has asked for the loom-room, and I have given it, since the loom-room is hers. She is Sister Aldith, weaver to this house these nineteen years, who has woven every shroud that has gone out of our yard, each one measured to the dead one's own cord. I enter her because the Rule says every soul under this roof who is not well is to be entered, and she is not well.

[b]Note to eleven hundred and six, the first night.[/b] She has taken the shroud off the loom. It was for the salt-carter in the second bed, measured to his cord, and he is not yet dead. She has begun to wrap it round herself from the feet. I asked her to stop. She said the measure was wrong and she was making it right.

[b]Intake eleven hundred and seven.[/b] A pilgrim of the Moor road, chest-sick, brought in on a carter's board. Bed: the third. Wrapped to the chin against the cold by Sister Ode, as I have ordered for every bed since the frost came. Disposition: to the road, the ninth day. He walked out.

[b]Note to eleven hundred and six, the second night.[/b] The cloth has reached her waist. There is more cloth round her than was on the loom. The shuttle is in her hand and the hand is under the cloth, and we hear it: the beat of a loom, from inside the wrapping, while the loom in the corner stands empty with its weights hanging still. The cloth is warm.

[b]Note, the fourth night.[/b] Wrapped to the mouth. Before the cloth took her mouth she asked that the yard not be dug for her and that she be laid on the loom. Refused: the Rule gives every soul of this house to the yard. She said the ground would not have her either.

[b]Intake eleven hundred and six, disposition.[/b] Dead at the lamp-hour of the fifth night, wrapped to the crown. To the yard the sixth morning, by Sister Ode and the gardener. I note that the shroud had no seam. A shroud is sewn shut over the head with nine stitches, by the weaver. This one was woven shut, as a sleeve is woven, and there was nobody outside it to weave.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The yard[/color][/font_size]
[b]The seventh morning.[/b] A corner of grey cloth above the soil at the head of the grave, a hand long, standing up the way a shoot stands. Cut with the yard-knife and pressed back under. The grave dug a hand deeper and filled.

[b]The eighth morning.[/b] Cloth above the soil at the head and at the foot both. The cut I made yesterday is whole, the threads knitted across the cut. Sister Ode has tried the cloth with the knife. Cut across the weft, it parts and is whole by morning. Cut along the warp, with the thread, it parts and stays parted. She has cut a strip the length of the grave along the thread and it has not healed. I have given the yard-knife to the gardener with that instruction: with the thread, never across.

[b]The ninth morning.[/b] The grave open. Open from beneath: the soil fallen in, as into a hollow, and nothing at the bottom. No cloth. No print in the soil of the yard. A drag, as of a hem, from the grave to the door of the long ward, and the door shut, and the drag going under it.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The long ward[/color][/font_size]
[b]Intakes eleven hundred and two, four, and five, disposition.[/b] Found at first grey wrapped to the crown in grey cloth with no seam, in their beds, dead, and warm through the cloth. These were the three who had thrown off their wrappings in the night, as the fevered do. Beds two, three, five and six, wrapped to the chin by Sister Ode at the lamp-hour, were untouched. The salt-carter in the second bed, whose shroud she took, lay with his own wrapping to his chin and slept through it and is alive. I write it plainly, so the next matron has it: she took the bare ones. She took none that had been wrapped first.

[b]What was seen.[/b] Sister Ode sat the ward and saw her come, and I take her words down as she gave them. She is long now. The cloth has pulled her. Her head bent under the beams of the ward, and the beams are two men high. The cloth goes before her along the floor, the length of a bed, and lies still; then it draws taut, from the far end; then she comes, and under the wrapping the loom beats faster. Where the cloth lies, do not step. When it draws taut, step back. She comes as far as the cloth and no further, and the cloth is longer each time. The pilgrims in the yard have a name for her already, which is the Long Sister, and I have let it stand, because it is kinder than mine.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Orders of this house from this day[/color][/font_size]
Every intake to be wrapped to the chin at intake, well or ill, pilgrim or sister. Cloth to be cut with the thread. The loom-room to be locked. The loom is beating in the locked room, and there is nobody at it, and the weights are swinging.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[b]Intake eleven hundred and eight.[/b] Hawise, matron of this house. Brought: on her own feet. By: nobody. Complaint: the cold has got into my hands and I can feel the measure of them. Bed: I will take the matron's, since it is empty. Wrapped to the chin by my own hand. Disposition:

[i](Below, in Sister Ode's hand:)[/i]

Still with us, in the matron's bed, wrapped to the chin, and I sit up with her. She asked me to finish the line and I cannot. The beat in the loom-room stopped at the lamp-hour. I had thought the beat was the worst thing. I know now what the worst thing is, and it is the quiet after it, and the yard-knife is on my knee, with the edge laid along the thread.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Hawise, matron, by the Rule; and after her, Ode, who took the broom[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Ledger of Attempts upon the Three at Ash Shore
pages.by: An exorcist's ledger, kept against a fee from the Warden-Crone at Maren's camp. The clerk at Four Wents copied it fair when the fee was settled and added the lines at the foot. I have stood outside the way-hearth at Ash Shore since the bricking, with wax in my ears, and felt the ash lift against the bricks on the hour, the way a chest lifts.
pages.bb:
Ledger of Hamo Sayer, exorcist, licensed at the crossroads of Four Wents, kept in his own hand in the matter of the three singers in the way-hearth at Ash Shore, against the fee agreed with the Warden-Crone: nine coppers the attempt, and the ninth attempt owed free, as the licence binds me.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The matter[/color][/font_size]
Three figures of grey ash, standing in the hearth-ash of the way-hearth, a hand high and no higher, shaped as singers stand: chins up, mouths open, hands at the sides. They do not fall when the ash is raked. They sing, and the song is three notes going down, the three that the grandmothers hum on the Moor, and the third note is held. It has been held since the pilgrims found them, which was the Shut Night. The fourth note should go up, the way a question goes up at its end. It does not come.

Whoever hears the third draws breath for the fourth, as a singer draws it, and does not let it go. The pilgrim who found them stood with his chest full until he fell. The one who dragged him into the yard breathed out there, and so did he. The book I was licensed on has a name for the three, which I will set down once: Hau'thrassith, which the book glosses as the ones who have drawn the breath for it. In this ledger they are the Three.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The attempts[/color][/font_size]
[b]The first.[/b] Means: I sang the fourth note myself, the question, loud, from the door. Result: they turned their heads to me, all three together, and the third note went on under mine, and I had drawn my breath for the next and could not let it out, and had the sense to fall backward through the door. Finding: a voice from outside them does not finish it. They want it finished from inside. Paid: nine.

[b]The second.[/b] Means: the small bell from the chapel on the heath road, which gives the fourth note, struck at the hearth. Result: the bell's note hung in the room and would not fade. By morning the bell was full of ash to the lip, and the ash would not pour. Paid: nine, less the bell.

[b]The third.[/b] Means: water. I raked the Three into a pail and poured the yard-butt over them. Result: they came apart as ash comes apart. At the lamp-hour the ash in the hearth stood up again, three, a finger taller than before. They grow by what fails. Paid: nine.

[b]The fourth.[/b] Means: I carried the hearth-ash in a sack a league onto the Moor and let it go on the wind at the Ashwake stones. Result: three singers in the hearth at Ash Shore at the lamp-hour, as before, out of ash that had not been there. I begin to think the ash is only what the note stands in, as a candle is what a flame stands in, and that I have been raking the candle. Paid: nine.

[b]The fifth.[/b] Means: wax in both ears, the warden's trick for the singing Gasps in the crypt. Result: I saw their mouths move and I did not fill. I walked to the hearth and put my hand through them. Warm; nothing more. A man who cannot hear the third does not draw for the fourth. Write that for the Warden-Crone: wax. And distance: I paced the note with the wax out, and at nine paces from the hearth-stone it is gone, as if cut, and at eight it is in your chest. Paid: nine.

[b]The sixth.[/b] Means: a deaf carter off the Four Wents road, paid double, to carry the hearth-ash out and away, since the deaf cannot be held. Result: he carried it out and the hearth was clean at the lamp-hour. The Three stood at the lamp-hour in the ash of his own fire, in his cart, on the Barrow road. He had not heard them and he had carried them. He is alive, I am told. Paid: nine, and nine to him.

[b]The seventh.[/b] Means: the fourth note sung by a purifier of the House of Eight Million, who can hold a breath past any Tithed and let it out past any. Result: she sang it. The Three closed their mouths. The hearth went cold through the stone. Every soul in the house let its breath go at once, nine of us, like a roof giving. Then a quiet I have not heard the like of. Then, at the lamp-hour, three notes going down, and the third held. She says the note cannot be finished by anyone who means to live after it, and she said it with her fan shut, which is how her House says the things it will not breathe in. Paid: nine. She took nothing.

[b]The eighth.[/b] Means: I sat the night by the hearth with the wax in and watched them. Result: findings only. Before they begin, which is on the hour, the ash lifts off the hearth-stone the width of a finger and hangs, as a chest lifts before a note. Anyone who sees the ash lift has that long to be nine paces off. And I counted their hands. I had not. Nine hands, three singers. Each has a third hand, and the third hand is held out toward the hearth-mouth, palm up, the way a singer asks the next voice to come in. Paid: nothing. I did not ask.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[b]The ninth, owed free.[/b] Means: I have the fourth note. I have had it since the second attempt, from the bell. It wants finishing from inside, so I will stand in the hearth with them, in the ash, with the wax out, and sing it at their height, bent double, with my own breath drawn for it. If it finishes, the house is clean and the licence is kept. If it does not finish, I ask the Warden-Crone to leave the ash where it lies and brick the hearth, since it is only ash, and to

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]The ledger stops at the foot of the leaf, and the next leaf is clean. The way-hearth at Ash Shore has four singers in it now, each a hand high, and the mouth of the fourth is open on a note that goes up and is held. The Warden-Crone has bricked the hearth and paid the nine to his sister. The pilgrims on the Moor hum the three going down and stop, and I know now why. — the clerk at Four Wents, who copied this fair and sang nothing[/color][/i][/indent]

pages.title: Discrepancy Entered Against the Fifth Wall, with the Inspection
pages.by: From the niche-tallies of the Fifth Ossuary, the tallier's leaf and the Warden's hand under it. The tallier who copied it for me asked, when he had finished, whether I had ever counted the same thing twice and had two numbers, and I told him the truth, which was yes, and he was glad, and I was not.
pages.epi: So long as a tallier has breath, they hold for the count.
pages.bb:
To the Warden of the Fifth Ossuary, from the tallier of the Fifth Wall, at the Feast of the Laying, the walls standing at their count save one.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The niche[/color][/font_size]
Fourth Stair, Fifth Wall, the two hundred and seventh niche from the stair-foot. Laid in the book as: Orsabet, called the Twin, of the lowlands, laid whole, two hundred and six, root eight, open. Beneath her line in the book a second line is scraped to the skin. The scraping is as old as the hand that laid her, which is older than any brother living, and it was done with care.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The count at the Feast[/color][/font_size]
Bones in the niche: two hundred and six, as laid. Standing in the niche: two.

I counted the standing three times, as the Rule requires, and had two each time. The bone count of the Fifth Wall is unchanged from last Feast. The standing count of the Fifth Wall is one over. The discrepancy is therefore in the standing, and the Rule makes no provision for it, since a frame stands once.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]What stood[/color][/font_size]
Two, shoulder to shoulder, facing the stair, as the laid must. Each whole to the eye at a glance. Each lacking, when looked at. The one on the left had the skull. The one on the right had none, and stood as the headless stand, patient. I moved my lamp from the left to the right. The one on the right had the skull. I had not seen it pass. There is a gap between a thing seen and the same thing seen again, and that is where it passed.

I set down what each lacked while my lamp was on it. The left wanted the right hand; the right wanted the left. The left wanted nine ribs; the right wanted three; between them, twenty-four. The right stood on its shins, set in the dust as a candle is set. Between them, in every pairing, two hundred and six. Neither was ever two hundred and six alone.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The inspection, the Warden present[/color][/font_size]
The Warden asked them to step down. One stepped down, whole, and stood on the stair with its hands folded. The other, in the niche, was a heap: a left foot, three ribs, the small bones of one hand, laid on the dust in the shape of somebody kneeling. The Warden asked the one on the stair to step up again. It did. The heap stood up into a frame as it did so, and the one that had stepped up was thin by what the other had taken to stand. They cannot both be whole. They take turns, and the turn is quicker than a lamp.

The Warden had me count the niche aloud, bone by bone, as at the Laying. I counted. For the two hundred and six of my count nothing moved. The lack stayed where it was; the skull stayed on the left; the thin one stayed thin. When I had said two hundred and six and drawn breath, the skull was on the right. The Warden had me count again, and again nothing moved while I had breath. He said: so long as a tallier has breath, they hold for the count, as the laid must; and he had me count until my voice went, and we left the niche as the lamp found it, the skull on the left, and I do not know what it was when the lamp was gone.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The old name[/color][/font_size]
The sweeper of the Fourth Stair, who is past speaking of most things, was brought to the niche. He put his thumb on the scraped line in the book, and then on the lintel of the niche, where a sign is cut in the script of the lower halls: two bones meeting at a joint, and the same again beside it. The talliers read that sign as the ones between. He said the two came up the stair together in a frost of a year nobody has, two sisters with one cord of knots between them, and asked to be laid together, and the brother who laid them did a thing the Rule did not forbid because the Rule had never thought of it. He laid one frame and wrote two names. Then the second asked that hers be scraped, so that the book should hold one. He said the lower-hall word for the sign, which I will not write, since it is two sounds and the second of them is a gap.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]On the low road[/color][/font_size]
I add, as the Warden bids me, that the knights of the low road report a thing they call the Miscount: two frames walking as one toward the lowland barrows, and what the one strikes with, the other has that moment lost. The arm goes out of the thin one as it comes into the whole one. A knight who watches the one that is emptying knows where the blow will come from. A knight of ours with breath enough counted them to a stand on Widow's Lane, aloud, from one, and walked past them on the two hundredth.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Entered[/color][/font_size]
The Warden rules: the niche is to be counted as laid, one frame, two hundred and six, root eight, open. The standing count of the Fifth Wall is to be entered as it stood last year. The scraped line is to stay scraped.

I have entered it so. I set down here, beneath the rule-line, where the book is read by no one aloud, that I went back through the book to see what last year's standing count had been entered from, and it was entered from the year before, corrected, and so back, in every hand, to the hand that laid them. The standing count of the Fifth Wall has been one over since the Laying of Orsabet, and every Feast since, every tallier has corrected it to the year before. We have counted her as one for longer than we have been counting.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Tallier of the Fifth Wall, written as Two Thousand Three Hundred and Forty. Root nine. Closed.[/color][/i][/right]
[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Feast following. Fifth Wall, two hundred and seventh niche: empty. Two hundred and six bones gone from the wall and the wall entered as last year. Prints on the Fourth Stair going down, in the dust, one set, each print laid twice, the second a little behind the first. Let the scraped line stay scraped. — the Warden, in his own hand, who counted the prints and will not give the figure[/color][/i][/indent]

pages.title: Inventory of the Sacristy, Taken at the Abbot's Order
pages.by: This lay in the sacristy press of the monastery on the Moor road, the one the pilgrims call Fallen, under a finger of ash that smelled of nothing at all. The brothers are gone, and the great bell is still in the tower; on a wind off the Moor the pilgrims below feel it in their teeth and hear nothing, and walk faster.
pages.bb:
Inventory of the sacristy of this house, taken at the Abbot's order on the third night after the Shut Night, every item within the sacristy door to be set down, with its condition and whence it came, and nothing left out for being strange. Twenty-seven items at the inventory before. Thirty-two at this.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of vessels and vestments[/color][/font_size]
[b]Items the first to the twenty-third.[/b] As the inventory before: the cups, the two plates, the box for the oil, the copes, the albs, the black for the dead. Condition: as before. I pass over them. They have made no sound, and have lost none.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of bells[/color][/font_size]
[b]Item the twenty-fourth.[/b] The great bell, in the tower, cast with the name of this house round the lip. Condition: whole. It has lost its note. Struck for the night office, it is felt in the floor and in the teeth, and gives nothing to the ear. The rope is whole and the beam is sound and the bell-founder from Four Wents says there is nothing wrong with it that he has a word for. Whence the loss: see Item the twenty-seventh.

[b]Item the twenty-fifth.[/b] The hand-bell of the office, brass. Condition: whole. Rings.

[b]Item the twenty-sixth.[/b] The bell for the dying. Condition: whole. Rings flat by one breath, as the brother from the Fen says every bell on the Hide does.

[b]Item the twenty-seventh.[/b] One bell, small, the size of a shut fist, of a grey metal that takes no shine from the cloth, without a tongue. Called by the brothers the Un-Bell, and by the one who carries it nothing, since he does not speak. Condition: whole. Whence: it came in out of the ash of the Moor on the Shut Night in the hand of Item the thirty-second, and was not asked for.

Note. It does not ring. Struck, it unrings. The last sound made in its hearing, if that sound has ended, is taken: out of the air, and out of the thing that made it. The great bell was rung for the night office on the Shut Night; the clapper fell into this bell; the great bell has not had its note since. Brother Osgar said the last word of the office and shut his mouth; the clapper fell; Brother Osgar has not had that word since. He comes to it in the office and his mouth works, and goes past the place, and the brothers go past it with him. It was struck once in the yard after the wind had dropped. The wind has not come back into the yard. The kitchen smoke goes straight up on the worst nights off the Moor.

Note, further. What has not ended, it cannot take. Brother Anselm was singing the whole of the office through, under his breath, when the clapper fell, and he lost nothing. He has not stopped singing since, waking and, the infirmarian says, sleeping. The brothers have learned it from him. This house hums.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of censers[/color][/font_size]
[b]Items the twenty-eighth and twenty-ninth.[/b] Two censers of black iron on chains, of no pattern of ours. Condition: lit. They have been lit since they came in, and the coals in them do not go down. Whence: Item the thirty-second carries them, one to each upper hand. Note: the smoke smells of nothing. It does not rise. Where the bell has taken a sound, the smoke stands in the air in the shape of what was taken. I have seen the shape of a word stand over Brother Osgar's stall from the night office to first light, like a breath on a cold morning that forgot to go.

[b]Item the thirtieth.[/b] The clapper of Item the twenty-seventh, carried loose in the lower right hand of Item the thirty-second. A finger-bone, long, with more joints than a finger has, of no shape I know. Condition: warm.

[b]Item the thirty-first.[/b] The rope of the great bell. Condition: whole. Nobody pulls it now. There is nothing to pull it for.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of persons[/color][/font_size]
The Abbot's order was that everything within the sacristy door be set down. He sleeps within the sacristy door, standing, between the press and the wall, and does not lie down, and so I set him down.

[b]Item the thirty-second.[/b] One Sub-Deacon. A priest of no order known to this house, in a cope of grey that was some colour once, with four arms. The upper two swing the censers. The lower left carries the Un-Bell by its crown, upright, as a cup is carried full. The lower right holds the clapper. His face is behind the smoke, which hangs before it like a veil and goes with him when he walks, so that nobody in this house has seen it, and the Abbot, who has stood close enough to see it, says he did not look. He has never spoken. He does not eat. He stands at every office at the foot of the great bell's rope and does not sing. The Abbot has not forbidden him the office. I believe the Abbot has tried, and that the words he tried with are among what is gone. Condition: I cannot say. Whence: the ash of the Moor, on the Shut Night, walking toward the gate with the bell already in his hand and the censers already lit.

Note on his manner, for the brothers. Before the clapper falls, the censers stop. Both. They stop at the top of the swing, with the chains straight out, against all nature, and hang there, and the smoke stands. Then the lower right hand opens. Then the sound, which is the sound of a bell heard from the wrong side of it. A brother who sees the censers hang has the time it takes to begin a sound, and should begin one, and not end it.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of what is missing from this house since the inventory before[/color][/font_size]
The great bell's note. Brother Osgar's last word. The wind in the yard. The sound of the gate, which opens and shuts and makes nothing. My own name as the Abbot says it: he said it in the cloister, and stopped, and the clapper fell, and he has called me sacristan since, and I answer to it. The inventory before had twenty-seven items. This has thirty-two, and it is shorter.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— The sacristan of this house, whose name the Abbot had[/color][/i][/right]
[i](Below, in another hand, smaller, pressed hard:)[/i]

Item the thirty-third. The night office. Condition: ended. Taken.

pages.title: A Letter from the Barrow Road, with Its Postscripts
pages.by: Folded in a bedroll made up beside a dead fire on the Barrow road, a day short of the Crypts, never sealed and never sent. The fire had been banked by someone who meant to come back to it. I have carried the letter to the village it names and could not find the door, and I have stopped looking for the door.
pages.bb:
Mother,

I write from the way-house at Four Wents, where the warden has lent me ink and a corner of his table and has not asked what I am looking at over my shoulder, which I take kindly. I am well. I have my feet and my coat and the cord. I will be at the Crypts in two days and I will light at the Long Candle for Ysolt, as I said I would, and then I will come home by the Moor road and you will have this from my hand before any carrier could bring it. I write it anyway. I want it written somewhere other than in me.

I went into the ring at Ashwake alone, as the old walkers say to. I will not tell you how it is in the stones; the old walker at the hearth there told me and she was right in every particular and I wish she had been wrong in one. I came up at the Barrow ring wet to the hair, and dry by the time I had my name back. Nine of us had gone in by ones from Ashwake. Ten of us stood up out of the ash at the Barrows.

The tenth is behind me. Three paces. She has been three paces behind me since I stood up. The others saw her before I did, because I cannot see her. I turn, and she is behind me still, three paces, whichever way I turn. I have turned fast. I have turned in a doorway, with the door-post against my shoulder. I have had a carter stand facing me and tell me what she did while I turned, and he says she turned with me, the way your shadow does when you try to step on it, and then he stopped laughing and would not walk with me after.

They call her the Late Sister on this road. Everybody knows the name and nobody will tell me who she is. The tender at the Barrow lantern says she comes to whoever comes up out of a ring alone, and that she is a sister to whoever she follows, whatever she is to anyone else. The old walker at Four Wents says something else, which I will put further down, where I can bear it.

She stops when I stop. She steps when I step. When I sit, the others say she sits, three paces back, on the ground, with her hands in her lap the way I sit. She does not eat. She does not speak. At the lantern-stones the flame leans back to her and never to me, and the tender did not like that, and wiped the glass twice.

What she looks like. I have asked everyone. The carter said: she has your walk. The tender said: she has your coat, and your cord, and the knot in it is in the same place. A pilgrim woman from the Fen road looked a long time and said: she has your face, only she is later than you. I asked what that meant. She said: your face is at noon and hers is at the lamp-hour. Then she asked me whether I had a sister, and I said I had, and she asked where, and I said at the Crypts, where I am going, and she went quiet, and I have not seen her since.

Mother, here is what the old walker said. She said the ring gives everyone back and keeps a little, and that sometimes the little it keeps has your coat on, and comes up three paces behind, and is as late as it is because that is how long the stones held it, and that it is you, three paces late, and it is catching up at the pace of a person walking. She said: do not look back for her. Each time you look back, she takes a pace while your head is turned, and gives it back when you face the road, out of courtesy, and one day she will not give it back.

The tender said one other thing, which I set down because it is the only thing anybody has told me to do. She said: three paces is her measure, and she keeps it by yours, so a gap wider than three paces she cannot cross on her own feet. At the Broken Bridge the middle plank was gone and the gap was four paces. I jumped it. The carter behind me said she stood at the brink and did not jump, and did not fall, and stood. For a day and a night she was gone and I walked with nobody behind me and I did not know how to do it. At the next ring-stone on the road, where the pilgrims step out, she was three paces behind me again, and the tender there said she looked as though she had been waiting.

I have not been able to think of a gap wider than three paces that lies between here and home.

So I have decided this. I will go on to the Crypts and light for Ysolt, with her behind me, since lighting for a sister is a thing a sister may stand behind. And then I will come home, and if two of us come up the lane, Mother, you are to look at the one in front and speak to her, and give the other nothing, and shut the door at three paces.

Your daughter, who came up,

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Ebba[/color][/i][/right]
[b]Postscript.[/b] The others have gone on. I am in the way-house with the door shut and she is three paces behind me, and the room is two paces deep. I have not worked out how, and I have stopped trying, and I am writing with my face to the wall.

[b]Postscript.[/b] I looked. Two.

[b]Postscript.[/b] The warden says she stands at my shoulder the way a lantern does, a little behind and a little to one side, and that I should let her carry it, whatever it is. He is kind. He has not turned round.

[b]Postscript.[/b] I looked. One.

[b]Postscript.[/b] She is warm at my back. She has my breathing. We breathe together or I fall out of step.

[b]Postscript.[/b] Mother, if two come

[b]Postscript.[/b] Late.

[i](Under the postscripts, in the same hand, a little later, pressed harder: Ebba.)[/i]

pages.title: Claim for Losses on the Salt Road, Itemised
pages.by: A fair copy from the reeve's roll at Four Wents, with the clerk's lines at the foot, which are in the roll too. I knew the claimant by sight before this and I know him by sight after, and he is the same man, and I have counted his carters myself on the road since, and I will not put my number against the reeve's.
pages.bb:
To the reeve of Four Wents, by the old right of the crossroads, the claim of Osric Vell, factor in salt and marrow-tallow, for losses on the salt road between the Salt Ford and this crossing, taken on the fourth night of the salt-run by the thing the carters call the Inventory, itemised as the reeve requires, with values in copper where a value can be set.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]How it came[/color][/font_size]
It stood at the tail of the last cart at the lamp-hour, where the road leaves the ford-stones. Tall as a laden cart, narrow, in grey like a clerk's, with a list. The list is a strip of something pale and long that comes down from its hand to the road and runs along the road behind it, and does not drag. It counts. It pointed at each cart, and each man in the traces, and each sack, with a finger as long as my forearm, and after each pointing there was the sound a pen makes on a dry leaf. What it pointed at once it passed over. What it pointed at twice went white with frost on the second pointing, and that it took, and the taking made no sound at all.

It counted me. I felt the count go over me the way a hand goes over a bolt of cloth, feeling for the flaw. It pointed at me once.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The items[/color][/font_size]
[b]Item the first.[/b] Marrow-tallow of Nine Stairs, forty cakes, sealed with the Order's thumb. Pointed at once each. Taken: none. Value: no claim. I set them down because the clerk says a claim is a list, and a list is all of it, or it is a story.

[b]Item the second.[/b] Salt of the white pans, eleven sacks. Pointed at once each. Taken: none. No claim.

[b]Item the third.[/b] The name of my second carter. He stood in the traces of the second cart and was pointed at twice, and I saw the frost come on his lips, and he stood with his mouth open. He answers to anything now, and to nothing, and we call him the second carter, and he comes. Value: I cannot set one. The clerk has written a line for it and left the line empty.

[b]Item the fourth.[/b] The shadow of Wat, fourth carter, who stood against the lantern and was pointed at twice. He casts none now. He complains of the cold on that side, and at the lamp-hour he stands where the others' shadows fall so as to be in one. Value: none set.

[b]Item the fifth.[/b] The right boot of every man, eleven boots. Pointed at twice, boot by boot, down the line of the traces. Taken off the feet without the feet being touched. The left boots it passed over. Value: eleven boots at four coppers, forty-four, which the clerk allows.

[b]Item the sixth.[/b] The heat of our fire. We had a fire lit on the ford-stones. It pointed at the fire twice. The fire burned on, and burns, and gives no warmth, and gives no light past a pace. Value: the firewood, three coppers.

[b]Item the seventh.[/b] My face in the ford-water. I knelt to drink and it pointed over my shoulder twice. I have no face in water now. In a glass I have one, grey, and later than I am; I move and it moves after. Value: none set. The clerk says a face is not goods, and I say he has not lost his.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[b]Item the eighth.[/b] I set this down because the clerk asked what was carried on the fourth cart that is no longer carried, since the axle of the fourth cart rides a hand higher than it rode at Ashwake, and the salt-sacks on it are pressed flat in one place, as under a sitter, and in the frost at the ford camp there was a set of prints beside the fourth cart that none of my men will own, bare, and small, and going nowhere. It was pointed at twice. It was on my cart and it was not on its list and it is gone, and the cart is lighter, and I did not know I carried it, and I am claiming for it. Value: I ask the reeve to set one. I cannot. I do not know what I had.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]What was spared, for the reeve's notice[/color][/font_size]
Three of the men were standing in the ford to the knee when it came, washing the salt off their legs, which is the carters' way at the end of a day. It pointed at them once, and again, and no frost came. It pointed a third time, and passed over them, and they have their names and both boots and their shadows and their faces. The water of the Salt Ford is Fen water run off, which wets nothing, and I think it could not find where they ended. Then it went on down the road toward the Barrows at the pace of a man reading, with the list running out behind it, and the frost on the road where the list had lain stayed till noon.

The carters call it the Inventory. A reader of the lodge at the ford said it has an older name, and that the Tallyman is its elder and keeps the great list, and this one keeps the lesser lists, and he offered me the name for a copper. I did not buy it. I have bought enough on this road.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Osric Vell, factor, who sets his mark here, and sets it with the left hand because the right is slow[/color][/i][/right]
[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]The reeve allows the fifth and sixth items, forty-seven coppers. Disallows the third, fourth and seventh as not goods. On the eighth the reeve has written in the margin: count your men. The claimant counted eleven, before the bench. The reeve has sent to the tender at the ninth stone, who keeps the tally of all who pass, for the number that set out with Vell. Twelve set out. The claimant says he has always had eleven men, and says it in the voice of a man who has always had eleven. The reeve has let the claim stand at the boots and the fire, and has entered the eighth item in the roll with no value against it, and the roll has been heavier in the hand since, and I carry it with both. — the clerk of the assize[/color][/i][/indent]

pages.title: Survey of the Fourth House on the Lane at Coldhearth
pages.by: Sent to the Warden-Crone at Maren's camp with the cord wound round it, and she gave it to me unwound, having read it once by daylight. From the lane the house is one storey, with the thatch down to a tall man's brow. I went at dusk. The window above the thatch was lit.
pages.epi: A closed traverse comes back to its pin.
pages.bb:
Survey made for the Warden-Crone at Maren's camp, who asked whether the empty hearths at Coldhearth could take pilgrims through the winter, by Adela, measurer to the reeve of Four Wents, lent for the purpose. Instruments: a cord of a hundred knots, waxed; a plumb on a thread; chalk; and my own pace, which is a hundred to the cord's hundred and has been checked against it every morning for eleven years.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The lane[/color][/font_size]
Thirteen doors, as the woodcutter says. Fourteen graves by the old stone, as he also says. One well, which nobody draws from. The woodcutter lives at the last house and asked me not to measure his, and I have not. Twelve doors stand open. The fourth from the stone stands shut, and the wood of it is warm to the back of the hand, the way a step is warm where someone has been sitting.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The house, outside[/color][/font_size]
Nine paces by seven. One storey. The ridge at a man and a half; the eaves at my brow. One door, south. Two windows, south, shuttered. I walked the outside with the cord close against the wall: thirty-two knots, which is nine and seven and nine and seven, as it should be. I set this down because it is the only measure in this report that comes back to its start.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The house, inside[/color][/font_size]
The ground floor is one room, eight paces by six within the walls. Hearth to the north, cold, with ash in it. A board with a bowl on it, and a spoon standing up in the bowl, as the woodcutter said. The ceiling at my raised hand.

There is a stair. It goes up out of the north-east corner, against the chimney-breast, fourteen risers. A house of this height has no room for a stair, and I stood at the foot of this one with my hand on the ceiling and the stair going up past my hand into a dark that was taller than the house.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The second floor[/color][/font_size]
Fourteen risers. At the head, a passage, two paces wide, boarded, running north. I ran the cord along the left-hand wall. Forty-one knots from the stair-head to the end of the passage, in a house nine paces long outside, and the end of the passage is a door. Doors off the passage: four on the left, three on the right, and the one at the end. I opened the first on the left. A room, five by four, a bed made up, with the shape of a sleeper still pressed in it and the blanket turned back as if the sleeper had just risen. I opened the second. The same, and the shape smaller. I did not open the third.

The windows of the second floor look out on nothing. I unshuttered one and put my hand out. No cold, no warm, no wall, no wind, nothing to touch. Grey, as the inside of your own eyelid is grey when you shut your eyes against a lamp. I drew the hand back and counted the fingers before I did anything else, and I had them all.

I walked the floor round with the cord against the walls to close the traverse, as a measurer does to prove a plan. A closed traverse comes back to its pin. Mine came back three knots short, at a door I had not passed, and my chalk pin was on the far side of the door, a pace off, on the floor of a passage I had just walked, and I had not walked past any door to reach it.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]The door at the end of the passage[/color][/font_size]
I give this door its own head because it is the one thing in the house that moved. It is a door of the pale wood of the Hollow Wood, which nobody at Coldhearth builds with, and it is warm. The leaf swells and sinks, slowly, as a sleeper's side does under a blanket. The hinges are three, and they are knuckles: pale, jointed, with a shine on the joints from use. The latch is a finger, curled. When I stood before the door the finger lifted. I had not touched it.

Beyond the door is a room that was never built. I say so as a measurer: it has a floor, of boards; it has no wall that I could reach with the cord, which I paid out straight from the door to its full hundred and it touched nothing; it has a ceiling I could not see; the light in it comes from no window and lies on the floor in the shape of a window anyway. There is a chair, facing the door, at the edge of the light. There was nobody in the chair. The cushion was pressed.

The door opens on its own. Before it does, the leaf draws in, the way a chest draws in before a word, and the knuckles turn in the jamb and you hear them, three dry sounds, from the top. Then it swings in. I think it means to shut behind whoever goes in, and I think the chair is for them.

A door cannot shut on a cord. I laid mine in the jamb before I went in, and kept the end in my fist, and went in along it as far as the chair, and came back along it, and the door swung to on the cord behind me as I came, and stood, pressing, the way a door presses on a foot that is in it, and could not close, and the knuckles went white. I took the cord out and it shut. It would not open again while my lantern stood in the passage. It opened when I set the lantern down the stair, out of its sight. It does not care to be seen into. Take a cord. Leave the lamp on the stair. Do not sit down.

[font_size=30][color=#dcd3c2]Findings for the Warden-Crone[/color][/font_size]
The house will take pilgrims. I do not advise it. The cord is three knots short since I came out, and I have measured it against my pace, which has held true for eleven years, and it is my pace that has changed. I am nine paces to what was eight.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Adela, measurer to the reeve of Four Wents. Cord returned, ninety-seven knots.[/color][/i][/right]
[i](In the Warden-Crone's hand, under the signature: She went back for the three knots. Her pace is in the frost on the lane. It goes to the fourth door, and in.)[/i]

pages.title: Incidents at the Grieving Stone, with Its Words
pages.by: The warden's own leaf, from his table at the Grieving Stone on the Barrow road, where his successor found it under a stone with the ink dry. The rest of the leaf below the ninth is clean. I have held it to a lamp and there is nothing scraped, nothing faded, nothing under; it is a leaf that was never written on past that line.
pages.bb:
To the reeve of Four Wents and to whoever holds the Barrow road after me: incidents at and about the Grieving Stone concerning the thing the pilgrims call the Apology, set down as they fell, with its words exactly each time, because the words are the whole of the matter.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]What it is[/color][/font_size]
It is the height of a tall man and stands as a man stands who has come to the door with bad news: bowed, hands folded before it, head down, so that the face is never given. Its coat is the grey of the Moor at the hour before light, with ash on the hem. It speaks low, and courteously, in the tongue of whoever stands before it, and it speaks first. Then it waits the space of the words said back. Then it does the thing. It has never done a thing it had not said sorry for, and it has never said sorry for a thing it did not then do, save once, which is the sixth incident, and the sixth is why I write.

The reader of the lodge at Tarn Hollow gave me its name for a copper. I have not written it. He said it twice, and the second time it was shorter.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The incidents[/color][/font_size]
[b]The first.[/b] The Turned Mound, dusk. Present: myself, a carter. It said to the carter: [i]I am sorry about your lamp.[/i] The carter's lantern went dark in his hand. The glass is clean. The tender at Ashwake has held it to her ear and says there is nobody in it now, and will not say where the soul went, and has not taken the lantern back onto the hook. Loss: one lantern, and whoever was in it.

[b]The second.[/b] Widow's Lane, full night. Present: two pilgrims; myself at twenty paces. It said to the elder: [i]I am sorry for your hand. The left.[/i] He has the hand. It is cold, and he cannot feel it, and it does what the right hand does a moment after the right hand has done it, so that he claps like a man who is late to the clapping.

[b]The third.[/b] The Grieving Stone, first grey. Present: myself alone. It said: [i]I am sorry, warden, for your sleep.[/i] I have not slept since. I do not tire. I write this at night, and at night the lane is very clear.

[b]The fourth.[/b] The Empty Ninth, noon. Present: a brother of the Pale Order with his column and his standing dead. It said to the brother: [i]I am sorry for the ninth.[/i] The brother's cord had two hundred and six knots. It has two hundred and five, and the cord is whole, with no cut end and no slack where the knot was. The brother said the count had fallen, and the fewer is the holier, and he thanked it. It stood a long time at that, bowed, with its hands folded, and then went down the lane, and the brother said to me that he had never seen one of them not know what to do.

[b]The fifth.[/b] The Turned Mound, dusk. Present: myself, and the tender from Ashwake, come to see about the first lamp. It said to her: [i]I am sorry for what I am about to say.[/i] Then it said her name. She has not been able to hear her name since. It is said to her and goes by her like a word in a tongue she does not have. She answers to the hook on her hut door, which I rap.

[b]The sixth.[/b] Widow's Lane, night. Present: a pilgrim woman of the Fen road; myself. It said to her: [i]I am sorry for your breath.[/i] She said: [i]You are forgiven.[/i] It stood. It said it again, the same words. She said hers again. It said; she said. I counted by the shadow of the Stone, which moves at night as it moves by day, and I had forty-one of each before the first grey, and at the first grey it bowed lower than I have seen it bow and went down the lane, and had not done the thing. Her breath is her own. I set it down as the one thing I have seen stop it. It waits for an answer, and the answer it waits for is the one that lets it go on, which is any answer at all, or none. The other answer holds it, so long as it is given each time, and you can say it faster than it can be sorry, and you must mean it.

[b]The seventh.[/b] Tried the sixth myself, at the Stone, at dusk. It said: [i]I am sorry for your left eye.[/i] I said: you are forgiven. It said: [i]I am sorry for your left eye.[/i] I said it again. On the ninth time it said: [i]I am sorry, warden. You do not mean it.[/i] It was right. The eye is in my head. It sees the Barrow road at another hour than the right eye does: by my left eye it is always first grey on the lane, and the lane is empty, and the frost on it has nobody's prints.

[b]The eighth.[/b] The Grieving Stone, found at first grey. Present: nobody, by its own account, since the words were cut in the face of the Stone when I came, fresh, with the grit still in the letters: I AM SORRY FOR THE STONE. The Grieving Stone has stopped. Whatever it was doing all these years that gave it the name, it has stopped doing, and the pilgrims who used to put their hands on it put them on and take them away again and look at their palms.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
Signed each night as the Rule of the roads requires, this being the eighth night and the lane empty by both my eyes.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Hewe, warden of the Barrow road at the Grieving Stone[/color][/i][/right]
[b]The ninth.[/b] This table, this night. It is behind me as I write; I hear the fold of its coat. It has said: [i]I am sorry for the rest of the page.[/i]

pages.title: The Shore-Log Kept at the Drowned Village
pages.by: The watcher's own book, out of the hut on the door-post stilts at the edge of the Drowned Village, where she kept the shore-stakes for the boatmen. The last lines are the boatman's, said to a Fan-Bearer who wrote them under. I took the book myself. The lantern on the step was not mine, and I did not wipe it.
pages.bb:
Shore-log of Kiyo, watcher of the stakes at the Drowned Village, kept for the boatmen and the Well-Shrine, who pay for it in bread. The shore of the Fen draws back from the Kneeling Arch a little every night of a season and comes back all at once in one night, and a boatman must know where it stands. So I write where it stands.

[b]Night the first of the watch.[/b] Shore at the Arch: nineteen paces. Water: clear to the floor. Nothing come up.

[b]Night the third.[/b] Shore: twenty-one paces. Something on the floor past the fourth stake. The Fen is clear to the floor and leaves nothing wet, and a drowned thing on the floor has the water on it like glass on a picture. This one has no water on it. The water stands off it a hand all round, and in the hand's width there is air, and in the air it stands, upright, on the floor of the Fen, with its face up. A drowned man's shape, long drowned, in a coat. I could not see the face for the air moving.

[b]Night the fifth.[/b] Shore: twenty-two paces. It is nearer by a stake. It drips. Nothing drips here. Nothing has dripped at the Drowned Village in my mother's life or mine; a thing comes out of this water as dry as it went in. It is wet, and the Fen will not take the wet off it. Where the drops fall on the floor of the Fen the floor goes dark, and stays dark. The boatman would not row past it. He says the drowned of the Fen lie down. This one stands.

[b]Night the sixth.[/b] The shore came back in the night. Nine paces at the Arch, and all my stakes in the water, and the water went round it. It stood where it had stood, in its hand of dry air, and the shore went round it as a stream goes round a post, and did not move it a finger. The boatmen have a word for it already: the Tideless. The Fen moves. It does not.

[b]Night the seventh.[/b] It came up the bank at the lamp-hour. Where it stepped, the reeds are wet. I touched one. Wet. I have not been wet in my life, and I stood with my finger up in the air and looked at it a long time. It carried a lantern. A lantern of the road kind, iron, with the glass whole and clean and nothing in it. No wick. No flame. Nobody. It went along the bank with the lantern at its shoulder, a little behind and a little to one side, as a lantern goes with its own. Then it went back down into the water by the fourth stake, and the hand of air closed round it, and the dark drops went down with it.

[b]Night the eighth.[/b] The lantern did not go down. It followed me home. A little behind, a little to one side, at the height of my shoulder, the way mine does. Mine went small as a bead the whole way and turned in its glass to face it, as a face turns, and stayed turned. It stopped at my salt. I keep salt on the sill because my mother kept it, and I had never known what for.

[b]Night the ninth.[/b] It is on the step at the salt. It has nothing in it, and it is darker than the dark round it, the way an open door is darker than a wall. The boatman came and looked from the bottom of the ladder and said: that is the Unlit; it has nothing of its own to burn, so what it burns is the one it follows; and it does not need to hurry. I asked him what it was for. He said what any lantern is for, which is to carry you back. I asked back where. He went down the ladder.

[b]Night the tenth.[/b] Shore: I did not go down. I slept on the step with the salt between us and woke at first grey with frost on me, and colder by a little, the way you are colder when a lantern has carried you and kept its share. The salt line is whole. I think it does not need to cross.

[b]Night the eleventh.[/b] Shore: twenty-four paces. The Tideless at the second stake with its face up and its hands open, as if to catch what drips from it. I watched it move, because I made myself. Before it steps, the hand of air round it closes to a finger, and the water goes dull round it like breath on glass. Then it steps. And it walks only where the shore has stood. Every stake I have ever set, and every stake my mother set, is a place it may walk, and it came up the bank to the line of the first stake my mother drove, where the shore has never come in all the years of this book, and stood with its toes at the line and dripped, and did not step over. Stand above the oldest stake. Write that for the boatmen.

[b]Night the twelfth.[/b] Shore: I did not go down. The Unlit is at the salt. Mine is a bead.

[b]Night the thirteenth.[/b] Mine is lit and the light does not reach the floor. The Unlit is brighter, and it has nothing in it. I have wiped the glass of mine and said her name to it and it has not grown. I have been wet since the seventh night and I have not dried.

[b]Night the fourteenth.[/b] Shore at the Arch: [ … ]. Water: clear. I am going down to the stakes to see where it stood, and I am taking neither.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Said by the boatman at the Iron Hook to the Fan-Bearer who came at the new moon, and written under by her. The watcher's hut had two lanterns on the step, the dark one and hers, and hers was a bead and would not grow. The Fan-Bearer took hers to the Well-Shrine. The dark one would not be carried, and did not need to be, and is not on the step now. The stakes stand. The shore is at nine paces. There is a wet place on the step the size of two feet, and it has not dried, and the salt is whole.[/color][/i][/indent]

pages.title: Visitation of the Chapel at Kenning Hollow, with Findings
pages.by: Carried down the old water-cut with the abbot's letter by the youngest of the Peak, and kept by the lowland priest who fed her, who gave me this leaf and kept the other. I have stood at the door of the chapel at Kenning Hollow since. The singing was going on. I did not count from the threshold, and I did not hold out a bowl.
pages.bb:
Visitation made by four brothers of the Gold Bell, by the abbot's leave, upon the chapel at Kenning Hollow, on report from the valley that the chapel had not sent up its bowl for three seasons. Set down by the fourth of the four, who carried the bowl, to be read at the lip of the east stone and given to the hand.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]The roll[/color][/font_size]
The chapel's roll gives one hundred souls who have given to the bowl, a hundred names, and against each the mark that the name was carried up. The roll is in the chaplain's hand. The chaplain's name is the hundredth. Over the chapel door, in the valley's old letters, is cut a word the valley reads as those who kneel together, and I write it once, as the abbot requires: Khaa-Qhanith.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]What we found at the door[/color][/font_size]
The door stood open as a mouth stands open at the end of a breath. The congregation was at office. We counted from the threshold, as the Rule requires: one hundred, kneeling, in ten rows of ten, all facing the east wall where the chapel bell hangs. None rose for us. None turned. The bell's rope lay coiled on the floor beneath it, under three seasons of dust.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Findings[/color][/font_size]
[b]First. Of the breath.[/b] A congregation breathes as a hundred breathe. This one breathed as one breathes. We stood in the door and listened to one chest the size of a chapel. The candles on the east wall leaned toward it on the in-breath and stood straight on the out.

[b]Second. Of the kneeling.[/b] The second of us went in among the rows, as the Rule allows, to lift a hem and see that the knees were on the boards and the boards whole. He lifted a hem. He asked me to write exactly what he found: there was no place where the one kneeling ended and the next began. Under the robes, from the first row to the tenth, the Hundred is one skin, grey, and warm, and the robes are laid over it in a hundred places as a cloth is laid over a long table. The knees are on the boards. The boards are worn through to the earth, and the earth under them is pale and jointed.

[b]Third. Of the singing.[/b] The office sung was the one syllable of our Rule. The syllable is a fence and the silence is the prayer. They have no silences. The syllable goes on, one voice out of a hundred mouths, and has gone on since the hundredth mark was made. The mouths are open and empty: there is no tooth in any mouth of the Hundred, and the gums are grey and smooth as the lip of a bowl.

[b]Fourth. Of the one at the east wall.[/b] At the east wall, beneath the bell, with its back to the Hundred, stands the one who leads the singing. It wears the chaplain's cope. It is taller than the chaplain was by a forearm, and the added length is in the neck. The valley calls it the Chorister of Teeth. We call it that also; the chaplain's name is given, and a given name is not said. When it turned to us it opened its mouth, and the mouth is lined to the throat with teeth in rows, more rows than a mouth has room for, and each time the Hundred's syllable rose a little, a tooth arrived in it. We did not see any tooth pass. We saw them arrive. It has the Hundred's teeth. It is taking them one by one, and the singing is one syllable sung through a hundred teeth by one mouth, and through none by a hundred.

[b]Fifth. Of the asking.[/b] The Rule of the visit says ask for one thing: a name, to carry up. The first of us held out the bowl and asked. The Hundred answered, in the one voice, and gave a name into the bowl. The name was mine. I gave it to the open hand at noon over the east stone in my ninth year on the stair, and the hand keeps nothing, as we are taught. The Hundred had it. I set this down. I do not set the name down; I have not got it, and the bowl has been heavier since.

[b]Sixth. Of the bells.[/b] Then it came toward us. It does not rise. The Hundred comes forward on its knees, as a tide comes up a flat shore, with the syllable going, and the Chorister's mouth shut for the first time: it does not sing while the Hundred moves, and a brother who sees that mouth close has the time it takes the first row to cross a flagstone. The first of us struck the small bell at his belt, once, and we struck ours, and in the silence after the four bells, which is the prayer, the syllable stopped. The Hundred had never had a silence set before it. It knelt still. The Chorister's mouth hung open and the teeth in it were quiet. We went out through the door backward, striking the belt-bells by turns, so that there should always be a silence in the room. At the gate we stopped striking. From inside, the syllable began again, lower. The chapel bell above them tolled once, by itself, flat by one breath.

[center][color=#8c6a37]❧[/color][/center]
[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Asked of the abbot[/color][/font_size]
That the chapel at Kenning Hollow be struck from the roll of the lower houses. That no brother go down to it in fewer than four, and that no bowl be held out at its door. That its roll be carried up entire and given to the open hand, the hundredth name first. That the fourth of the four, who writes this, be let go up to the east stone at noon and stand there until the hand has taken back what the Hundred gave him; and if the hand will not take it a second time, that he be let sit on the landing with the bowl across his knees, and wait.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— The fourth of the four, who carried the bowl, and set it down to write[/color][/i][/right]
[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]Granted, all. He went up at noon. The hand took it. He came down lighter and could not say what the chapel was called. Kenning Hollow is struck from the roll. The roll is one name longer than it was, at the foot, in no hand of ours, and against it the mark. — the abbot, by his sign, which is an open palm[/color][/i][/indent]
